title: Happy 60th Birthday, ChatGPT
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Marking ChatGPT's first birthday, Dan Meyer places it inside a much older lineage of education-technology hype, quoting Patrick Suppes (1966), George Boehm (1960), and Simon Ramo (1957) making essentially the same promises - personalized machine tutors, transformed outcomes, solved teacher shortages - that Sal Khan and McKinsey are making about generative AI today. He argues that a year in, generative AI's classroom presence is thin: a few high-profile pilots (Khanmigo in Newark, a $40k/year private school) and vague aggregate usage numbers, not the sustained daily uptake that characterized genuine edtech shifts like graphing calculators or interactive whiteboards. Meyer's central claim is that education technologists keep misdiagnosing schooling as a "content challenge" - a matter of delivering the right material to the right student - when it is actually a "connection challenge": connecting students to the purpose of school, to each other, and to belief in their own capability. He credits computers and the internet with real transformative potential precisely because they are connective by nature, but warns that realizing it requires accounting for student needs that resist abstraction into machine-operable inputs. The piece closes on a personal note: Meyer plans to spend 2024 building a small AI feedback tool while doubling down on direct classroom work rather than edtech commentary, saying generative AI has taught him more about the limits of technology than about its promise.
points: Meyer lines up a century of confident predictions - from 1957's automatic teaching machines to 2023's AI tutors - and shows they all promised the same things: personalization, equity, and transformed outcomes, none of which arrived on schedule.

He argues generative AI's actual 2023 classroom footprint (a handful of pilot programs and aggregate sign-up counts) falls well short of the sustained, returning daily use met by earlier technologies like graphing calculators or interactive whiteboards.

His central reframe: schooling's core problem is a "connection challenge" - connecting students to the value of learning and to each other - not a "content challenge" that AI content delivery can solve.

Meyer credits generative AI with sharpening his own thinking about teaching more than with transforming his classroom, saying he's redirecting 2024 energy toward classroom video and professional learning rather than edtech evangelism.
quotes: In each century—this one and the last—futurists have predicted that new technologies will receive widespread usage in schools, ensure equitable access to education, allocate teacher labor more effectively, and transform student outcomes.

Shouldn’t we see the kind of deliberate and sustained uptake of generative AI in education that we saw with photocopiers, graphing calculators, digital projectors, interactive whiteboards, personal computers, and the internet itself?

Futurists have made this same bet on technology for 100 years only to see the dice come up snake eyes every time. That’s because futurists misunderstand the challenge of education as a content challenge

But education is a connection challenge. Education is, first, the challenge of connecting students to the project of schooling, investing them in its goals and processes while recognizing that many students have found those goals alienating

Computers and the internet are connective by their nature and therefore offer lots of transformative possibilities for education. But we will only see the kind of transformation imagined by our leading futurists if they’re able to control for a host of personal student characteristics

Our current research suggests that 20 to 40 percent of current teacher hours are spent on activities that could be automated using existing technology. That translates into approximately 13 hours per week that teachers could redirect
